Federation’s affiliate and the bank management regarding the fact that the exercise of identifying the messengerial 
vacancies as on 3l.l2.994 has since been completed by central office and thereby 403 messengerial vacancies were 
sanctioned to the circle of the Management bank and it was agreed that these vacancies may be filled from 989 panel 
of temporary employees after effecting conversion from full time non-messengerial staff in the usual manner and the 
agreement was reached upon. Further, it was agreed between the Federations affiliate and the management bank 
that in terms of the settlement dated 30.7.996 both the panels of temporary employees and daily wagers /casual 
employees would lapse on 3.3.997. 


37. The Workman has contended that the empanelled list prepared by the Respondent management for 
appointment of temporary and daily wage Workers to the permanent post cannot lapse unless until it is exhausted by 
appointing all the empanelled persons and it should continue even after 3.3.997, i.e., the date fixed for the lapse of 
panel. It is undisputed that the date of lapse of empanelled list of Workmen has been fixed to 3.3.997 as 
mentioned in the settlement dated 30.7.996, and agreed between the parties. It is settled law that and once the life 
of panel list lapses on the date as agreed between the parties it cannot be extended beyond that date. In the instant 
case the panel list of the workmen was valid upto 3.3.997 in view of the terms and conditions enumerated in the 5" 
Settlement entered into between the parties. As the lapse of panel i.e., 3.3.997 has been agreed by State Bank of 
India and State Bank of India Staff Federation through 5" Settlement, the Workman is not competent to challenge the 
same. 


In this context I would like to take reference of the decision of the apex court in the case of Syndicate Bank and Ors 
vs. Shankar Paul and Ors , AIR 997 SC 309], therein the Hon’ble Apex Court have held:- 


[भाग ए---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मार्च 28, 2026/चैत्र 7, 948 20I 


“Till 7962, the branches of the appellant Bank in Calcutta region were recruiting persons locally to work as 
temporary attenders in leave vacancies. In view of the revised procedure prescribed by the Government of India in 
respect of such temporary appointments, the Calcutta regional office of the appellant Bank issued a circular to all of 
its branches on /4.6./982, instructing all the branches under it to discontinue the old practice from /.6./982 and 
appoint only empanelled candidates. The regional office was to prepare a panel of eligible candidates, after calling 
names from the local/district employment exchange, and split it up branch-wise. Following that new procedure yearly 
panels were prepared thereafter. Names of the Respondents were for the first time included in the panel prepared for 
the period 7.2. /967 to 6.2. /966, By its letter dated 7.2,/967 the Bank had informed the Respondents that the panel 
was valid for one year only and that inclusion of their names in the panel was not to confer on them any right to seek 
permanent appointment in the service of the bank. Considering the object with which the panel was prepared and the 
fact that it was an yearly panel expiring on 6.2, /966, we are of the opinion that the Respondents did not get any right, 
because of inclusion of their names in the said panel, for permanent absorption in the service of the Bank. Whatever 
conditional right they had came to an end with the expiry of the panel. The claim of the Respondents, as contained in 
the writ petition was thus misconceived and therefore the learned single Judge and the Division Bench, when it first 
decided the appeal, were right in dismissing the writ petition and the appeal respectively.” 


Thus, in view of the above law laid down by the Hon’ble Apex Court and in view of the terms and conditions of the 
5‘ Settlement the contention of the Workman that empanelled list should continue even after 3.3.997 till the last 
Workman in the panel is absorbed is not tenable. The contention of the Workman is baseless in view of recital in 
the settlement. Therefore, in view of the fore gone discussion and finding given at Point No. I regarding binding 
nature of Settlements and terms and conditions enumerated therein, in view of the provision contained u/s.|8() of the 
I.D. Act, 947, I am of the considered view that life of panels lapsed on 3.3.!997 in view of terms of settlement 
dated 30.7.996 and plea of Workman that the panel shall continue even after 3].3.]997 till last man absorbed has 
no legal force and same is untenable. 


38. Undisputedly, settlement agreement dated 30.7.!996 was executed between the State Bank of India and 
State Bank of India Staff Federation and in that settlement it was agreed that both the panels of temporary employees 
and daily wagers/ casual employees will be used for filling vacancies existing as on 3.2.994 as per the norms 
agreed between the bank and the Federation. These empanelled workmen were to be given a chance for permanent 
appointment in the bank against vacancies arising up to December 994 whereas the daily wagers/ casual employees 
were to be considered against the vacancies arise from January 995 to December 996, whereby the said panel 
would lapse. It was agreed that the vacancies falls upto 3.3.!997 shall be filled before the empanelled list is 
allowed to lapse. Thus, the claim of the Workman to the post of permanent non-messenger in the Respondent 
management was subject to the availability of the sanctioned post and vacancies arising upto 3.3.997. The 
workmen given chance to the permanent post were seniors in number of working days in panel list and Workman 
herein was junior to those workmen. Therefore, Workman could not be given absorption to permanent post being 
junior to other workmen in the panel list. 


39. In this context the Workman witness १५७] was cross examined by the Respondent counsel and in the cross 
examination the witness WW states:- 


“I applied in response to the advertisement issued by the bank as per the settlement entered intoby the union with the 
bank..... Further, witness states, The vacancies of messengers were filled up with the temporary messenger and non- 
messengers whose names were kept in the panel. It is true that the vacancies were filled up following the order of 
their seniority in the panel. Further witness states, Iam not having any document to show that any person having 
less no.of days of service than me ws given appointment on regular basis in the bank.” 


Thus, from the above statement of the Workman witness ४४७] it is clear that the panel was prepared in terms of 
various settlements entered into between Staff Federation of State Bank of India and State Bank of India and it was 
prepared on the basis of number of days of work put in by the temporary employees. Further, the Workman himself 
admitted that some of the temporary employees whose names were included in the panel were given regular 
appointment in the bank in order of their seniority in the panel and he is not having any document to show that any 
person who worked for less number of days than the Workman was given appointment in the bank. Therefore, the 
allegation of the Workman that the regular appointment has been made by the bank from the panel list in breach of 
the terms of the settlement and violation of seniority of panel list is not proved by this evidence of WWI. Thus, 
there is no evidence on record that bank has given the appointment to the temporary employees as well as daily 
wagers from the panel list 989 and 992 in breach of seniority of the temporary employees in the list. There is no 
evidence of jumbling in the panel list to make appointment of any permanent Workman in breach of the seniority. 
Therefore, I am constrained to hold that the Respondent Management has appointed the workmen from panel list in 
order of seniority and there is no jumbling of workmen in the panel list before it got lapsed on 3.3.997, 


40. However, Workman has taken the plea that the panels of Workmen for absorption in the employment of the 
Respondent banks (panels of temporary employees and daily wagers) has been lapsed on 3.3.997 in contravention 
of terms of settlement as the object of preparing the entire empanelment of temporary and daily wagers was to 
provide them permanent employment and till the both the panel lists exhausted the panel list cannot be lapsed on 


202 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MARCH 28, 2026/CHAITRA 7, 948 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


3.3.997 and the date of lapsing of the panel on 3.3.997 has been fixed by the Respondent arbitrarily without any 
authority. 


4l. In this context, the perusal of Settlement dated 30.7.996 reveals that the 5" Settlement dated 30.7.996 
was entered under Section 2(p) and 8(l) of I.D. Act, 947 read with Rule 58 of Industrial Dispute (Central) Rules 
957. This settlement has been entered into by the competent parties and in this settlement parties thereto agreed 
that both the panels of temporary employees and daily wagers/casual employees will lapse on 3.3.997. Thus the 
date of lapse of panel was fixed by both the parties with consensus under the settlement dated 30.7.996 and same is 
binding upon the Workman under the provision of Section !8(l) of LD. Act, 947. Moreover, this issue of binding 
force of the settlement dated 7..987, 6.7.988, 27.0.988 and 9..99 has already been discussed, decided at 
finding in Point No.I of this award. However, the legality and validity of the aforementioned settlement has not been 
challenged by the Workman before any competent forum. Thus, claim of Workman that the date of lapse of panel 
i.e., 3.3.997 has been fixed arbitrarily by the Respondent bank is untenable. As regard the claim of Workman for 
his absorption to the permanent post it is settled law that the Workman can not claim his regularization to permanent 
post merely on the basis of number of working days. 


42. In this context the reference of the decision of Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Oil and Natural Gas 
Corporation vs Krishan Gopal 2020(3) SCALE 272, date of decision 7.2.2020 is relevant therein Hon’ble 
Supreme Court have has laid down principle regarding regularization of the Workman on permanent posts. Hon’ble 
Supreme Court have laid down the prepositions of regularization of the workmen to permanent post is as under:- 


“(i) Wide as they are, the powers of the Labour Court and the Industrial Court cannot extend to a direction to order 
regularisation, where such a direction would in the context of public employment offend the provisions contained 
in Article /4 of the Constitution; 


(ii) The statutory power of the Labour Court or Industrial Court to grant relief to workmen including the status of 
permanency continues to exist in circumstances where the employer has indulged in an unfair labour practice by not 
filling up permanent posts even though such posts are available and by continuing to employ workmen as temporary 
or daily wage employees despite their performing the same work as regular workmen on lower wages; 


(iii) The power to create permanent or sanctioned posts lies outside the judicial domain and where no posts are 
available, a direction to grant regularisation would be impermissible merely on the basis of the number of years of 
service; 


(iv) Where an employer has regularised similarly situated workmen either in a scheme or otherwise, it would be open 
to workmen who have been deprived of the same benefit at par with the workmen who have been regularised to make 
a complaint before the Labour or Industrial Court, since the deprivation of the benefit would amount to a violation of 
Article /4, and 


(v) In order to constitute an unfair labour practice under Section 2(ra) read with Item /09 of the Vth Schedule of the 
ID Act, the employer should be engaging workmen as badlis, temporaries or casuals, and continuing them for years, 
with the object of depriving them of the benefits payable to permanent workmen. 


Thus, in view of the principles laid down by the Hon’ble Supreme Court as discussed above, in the instant matter the 
Workman utterly failed to prove his claim by adducing any documentary or oral evidence that the employer has 
indulged in unfair labour practice by not filling the permanent posts even though such posts are available and by 
continuing to employ workmen as temporary or daily wage employees despite their performance was the same work, 
as regular workmen on lower wages. 


43. Respondent has contended that all the vacancies exist and arise upto 3!.3.!997 has been filled up from the 
panel list in order of seniority and no vacancy exists or arises as on 3.3.997 remained unfilled. Further, it is 
contended that as per terms of settlement the life of panel lists has been lapsed on 3.3.997, hence, there is no 
occasion to extend the life of panel lists beyond 3.3.!997. However, the workman failed to prove contrary by any 
evidence to the aforesaid contention of the Respondent that the vacancies were existing as on 3!.3.997 and the 
workman was not given absorption to the permanent post in order of his seniority. It is settled law that the power to 
create permanent or sanctioned post lies outside the judicial domain and where no posts are available, a direction to 
grant regularization would be impermissible merely on the basis of the number of years of service. Therefore, the 
claim of the workman on this ground also not acceptable. 


44. Further, as per the of settlement, panel was prepared for absorption of the workmen on the permanent posts 
has already been lapsed on 3!.3.997 and the vacancies existing and arising upto 3.2.994 and upto 3.3.997 as 
settlement dated 30.7.996 has been filled up from the panel by appointing the workmen as per seniority in the panel 
list. Workman witness WW in his cross examination has himself admitted this fact that, some of the temporary 
employees whose names were included in the panel were given regular appointment in the bank in order of their 
seniority in the panel. The Workman failed to show that there was any breach of terms of settlement has been 
committed by the Respondent in appointment to permanent post from aforesaid panel list. 


[भाग ए---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मार्च 28, 2026/चैत्र 7, 948 20I3 


45. As discussed in preceding paragraph of this Award, the life of the panel has not been extended beyond 
3.3.997, by any further settlement hence, the panel list in which name of the Workman was included got expired 
on 3I.3.997. It is not the case of the Workman that Respondent has regularized similarly situated workmen either in 
the scheme or otherwise and the Workman has been deprived of same benefit on par with those workmen or the 
vacancies remained unfilled on the date of lapse of panels i.e., 3.3.997, Industrial Tribunal has no jurisdiction to 
extend the date of lapse of panel i.e., 3.3.997. This Tribunal can not order for regularization of workmen to the 
permanent post in contravention of the provision of Article l4 of the Constitution of India. 


In the case of Mahboob Deepak vs. Nagar Panchayat Gajraula & Anr, Civil Appeal No.5875/2007 date of 
judgement 3.2.2007, Hon’ble Supreme Court have held:- 


“8. Respondent is a Local Authority. The terms and conditions of employment of the employees are governed by a 
statute and statutory rules. No appointment can be made by a Local Authority without following the provisions of the 
recruitment rules. Any appointment made in violation of the said rules as also the constitutional scheme of equality as 
contained in Articles /4 and /6 of the Constitution of India would be a nullity. 


9. Due to some exigency of work, although recruitment on daily wages or on an ad hoc basis was permissible, but by 
reason thereof an employee cannot claim any right to be permanently absorbed in service or made permanent in 
absence of any statute or statutory rules. Merely because an employee has completed 240 days of work in a year 
preceding the date of retrenchment, the same would not mean that his services were liable to be regularized.” 


Therefore, in view of the law laid down by the Hon’ble Apex Court, the claim of the Workman for absorption merely 
on the basis of number of day of work in the Respondent bank Branch is not acceptable. As regard plea of the 
Workman that the Workman should have been given employment even after 3.3.997 as temporary Workman, it is 
the discretion of Respondent to engage the Workman depending upon availability of work and this Tribunal can not 
direct the Respondent to engage the Workman in the absent of such rule/scheme. 


46. In view of principle laid down by Hon’ble Apex Court as discussed above, in the instant matter Workman 
utterly failed to establish the fact of rendering continuous service for a period of 240 days of service within a period 
of 2 calendar months commencing and coming backward from relevant date i.e., the date of retrenchment, if has he 
would be denied to be in continuous service for a period of one year. Therefore, the provision contained under 
Sec.25F of retrenchment is not applicable to Workman. 


Counsel for Workman has relied upon number of decisions of Hon’ble High Court and Hon'ble Supreme Court and 
few of them are discussed herein:- 


In the case of F.C.I., vs. Kamdhenu Cattle Feed Industries 993 () SCC 7], therein Hon’ble Supreme Court have 
held:- 


“7. In contractual sphere as in all other State actions, the State and all its instrumentalities have to conform to Article 
_4 of the Constitution of which non-arbitrariness is a significant facet. There is no unfettered discretion in public law: 
A public authority possesses powers only to use them for public good. This impose the duty to act fairly and to adopt 
a procedure which is ‘fairplay in action’. Due observance of this obligation as a part of good administration raises a 
reasonable or legitimate expectation in every citizen to be treated fairly in his interaction with the State and its 
instrumentalities, with this element forming a necessary component of the decision making process in all State 
actions. To satisfy this requirement of non- arbitrariness in a State action, it is, therefore, necessary to consider and 
give due weight to the reasonable or legitimate expectations of the persons likely lo be affected by the decision or else 
that unfairness in the exercise of the power may amount to an abuse or excess of power apart from affecting the bona 
fides of the decision in a given case. The decision so made would be exposed to challenge on the ground of 
arbitrariness. Rule of law does not completely eliminate discretion in the exercise of power, as it is unrealistic, but 
providers for control of its exercise by judicial review.” 


In the case of State Bank of India, R.O., Vijayawada vs. Industrial Tribunal, Hyderabad WP ४०.।9३/997, 
therein Hon’ble High Court have held, 


“Sri Krovvidi Narasimham, the learned counsel for the 2" respondent contends, supporting the award that it was a 
permanent vacancy and even though the 277 respondent was appointed on temporary basis, his services were not 
liable to be terminated and he was to be regularised into service on permanent basis. Shastry award warrants that no 
temporary appointment can be made to a permanent post. But the matter is now covered by two division bench 
judgements dated 26, //./9866 in W.A. No.79 of /966 and 25.6. /9867 in W.A. No.270 of /962, The ratio decided in the 
two judgements is to the effect that there cannot be any mandate to appoint employees on permanent basis when the 
requirement was for appointment on temporary basis. But it is held in the said judgements that when a temporary 
appointee is ousted from service and not for misconduct and, if again temporary appointment is to be made, then, the 
case of such temporary appointee who was ousted, has got to be considered in accordance with Sec. 25-H of 
the Act.”

In the case of State of Haryana and others vs. Piara Singh and others. 992 (4) SCC 8, therein Hon’ble

44, Now the Authority constituted under Section 4/(/) of the Act is an authority with very limited jurisdiction. It can

The Tribunal thought that the question of the quantum of membership of the 2nd Respondent did not call for a finding

that this view of the Tribunal has led it to approach the matter in an entirely erroneous manner. The Tribunal is, 
rightly enough, conscious that under section /6 (/) of the Industrial Disputes Act the settlement was binding on the 
company and the members of the 3rd Respondent union. Even so, the Tribunal devoted nearly half of its order in 
scanning the evidence given by the company and Respondent No. 3 to find out whether the terms of the settlement had 
been explained by the President of the union to the workmen or not and whether the workers voluntarily accepted the 
settlement knowing all the "consequences". This to our mind is again an entirely wrong approach. 


“When a recognised union negotiates with an employer the workers as individuals do not come into the picture. It is 
not necessary that each individual worker should know the implications of the settlement since a recognised union, 
which is expected to protect the legitimate interests of labour, enters into a settlement in the best interests of labour. 
This would be the normal rule. We cannot altogether rule out exceptional cases where there may be allegations of 
mala fides, fraud or even corruption or other induce- ments. Nothing of that kind has been suggested against the 
President of the 3rd Respondent in this case. That being the position, prima facie, this is a settlement in the course of 
collective bargaining and, therefore, is entitled to due weight and consideration. 


It is not possible to scan the settlement in bits and pieces and hold some parts good and acceptable and others bad. 
Unless it can be demonstrated that the objectionable portion is such that it completely outweighs all the other 
advantages gained the Court will be slow to hold a settle- ment as unfair and unjust. The settlement has to be 
accepted or rejected as a whole and we are unable to reject it as a whole as unfair or unjust. Even before this Court 
the 3rd Respondent representing admittedly the large majority of the workmen has stood by this settlement and that is 
a strong factor which it is difficult to ignore. As stated elsewhere in the judgment, we cannot also be oblivious of the 
fact that all workmen of the company have accepted the settlement. Besides, the period of settlement has since expired

improvements. These factors, apart from what has been stated above, and the need for industrial peace and harmony 
when a union backed by a large majority of workmen has accepted a settlement in the course of collective bargaining

and order that the award of the Tribunal shall be substituted by the settlement dated October /6, /973, The said 
settlement shall be the substituted award. The appeal is disposed of accordingly. There will be no order as to costs.”

Section 25F provides:- 


Conditions precedent to retrenchment of workmen.- No Workman employed in any industry who has been in

(a) the Workman has been given one month' s notice in writing indicating the reasons for retrenchment and the period

(b) the Workman has been paid, at the time of retrenchment, compensation which shall be equivalent to fifteen days' 
average pay for every completed year of continuous service] or any part thereof in excess of six months; and 


(c) notice in the prescribed manner is served on the appropriate Government or such authority as may be specified 
by the appropriate Government by notification in the Official Gazette]. 


Compensation to workmen in case of transfer of undertakings. 
Section 25B defines the term continuous service which provides 
Definition of continuous service.- For the purposes of this Chapter,-- 


(2) a Workman shall be said to be in continuous service for a period if he is, for that period, in uninterrupted service, 
including service which may be interrupted on account of sickness or authorized leave or an accident or a strike 
which is not illegal, or a lock- out or a cessation of work which is not due to any fault on the part of the Workman; 


(2) where a Workman is not in continuous service within the meaning of clause (7) for a period of one year or six 
months, he shall be deemed to be in continuous service under an employer-- 


(a) for a period of one year, if the Workman, during a period of twelve calendar months preceding the date with 
reference to which calculation is to be made, has actually worked under the employer for not less than-- 


(i) one hundred and ninety days in the case of a Workman employed below ground in a mine; and 
(ii) two hundred and forty days, in any other case; 


In order to prove the fact of 240 days of service within !2 months of a calendar year just preceding from the date of 
termination, the initial burden of proof lies upon the Workman and the Workman has to prove this factum by 
adducing his oral as well as documentary evidence in support of his claim. 


Further, how to calculate 240 days of service by the Workman in a calendar year. In this context the reference of 
decisions of Hon’ble Supreme Court is relevant and the same are discussed below:- 


In Rajasthan State Ganganagar S. Mills Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan and Anr. (2004) Apex Court held: 


"It was the case of the Workman that he had worked for more than 240 days in the year concerned. This claim was 
denied by the appellant. It was for the claimant to lead evidence to show that he had worked for 240 days in the year 
preceding the date of his termination. He has filed an affidavit. It is statement which is in his favor and that cannot be 
regarded as sufficient evidence for any Court or Tribunal to come to the conclusion that in fact the claimant had 
worked for 240 days in a year These aspects were highlighted in Range Forest Officer v. S.T. Hadimani (2002 (3) 
SCC 25. No proof of receipt of salary or wages for 240 days or order or record in that regard was produced. Mere 
non-production of the muster roll for a particular period was not sufficient for the Labour Court held that the 
Workman had worked for 240 days as claimed."

In Municipal Corporation, Faridabad v. Siri Niwas (2004 (8) SCC 95), held "the burden was on the Workman to 
show that he was working for more than 240 days in the preceding one year prior to his alleged retrenchment." In 
MP. Electricity Board v. Hariram (2004 (8) SCC 246) the position was again reiterated in paragraph I! as follows: 
"The above burden having not been discharged and the Labour Court having held so, in our opinion, the Industrial 
Court and the High Court erred in basing an order of reinstatement solely on an adverse inference drawn 
erroneously ..” 


In the case of Manager, RBI, Bangalore vs. S Mani (2005) SCC Page 00, the 3 Judges Bench of the Apex 
Court held that "the initial burden of proof was on the Workman to show that he had completed 240 days of service." 


Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Mohan Lal vs Management BEL 98 SCC page 225 has laid down the 
principle that how to count 240 days of service within one year itis held: "Clause (2)(a) provides for a fiction 
to treat a Workman in continuous service for a period of one year despite the fact that he has not rendered 
uninterrupted service for a period of one year but he has rendered period of 240 days during the period of /2 
calendar service for months counting backwards and just preceding the relevant date being the date of retrenchment. 
In other words, in order to invoke the fiction enacted in clause (2)(a) it is necessary to determine first the relevant 
date, ie the date of termination of service which is complained of as retrenchment. After that date is ascertained. move 
backward to a period of /2 months just preceding the date of retrenchment and then ascertain whether within the 
period of !2 months, the Workman has rendered service for a period of 240 days. If these three facts are affirmatively 
answered in favor of the Workman pursuant to the deeming fiction enacted in clause (2)(a) it will have to be assumed 
that the Workman is in continuous service for a period of one year and he will satisfy the eligibility qualification 
enacted in Section 25-F" 


“4, We have already extracted section 25B since its amendment and the change in language is the legislative 
exposition of which note must be taken. In fact, we need not further dilate upon this aspect because in Surendra 
Kumar Verma_and Ors. v. Central Government Industrial-cum-Labour Court, New Delhi and Anr., Chinnappa 
Reddy. J., after noticing the amendment and referring to the decision in Sur Enamel and Stamping Works (P) 
Ltd case, held as under: 


"These changes brought about by Act 36 of /964 appear to be clearly designed to provide that a Workman who has 
actually worked under the employer for not less than 240 days during a period of twelve months shall be deemed to 
have been in continuous service for a period of one year whether or not he has in fact been in such continuous service 
for a period of one year. It is enough that he has worked for 240 days in a period of /2 months, it is not necessary that 
he should have been in the service of the employer for one whole year." 


In a concurring judgment Pathak J. agreed with this interpretation of section 25B(2). Therefore, both on principle 
and on precedent it must be held that section 25B(2) comprehends a situation where a Workman is not in employment 
for a period of 72 calendar months, but has rendered service for a period of 240 days within the period of /2 
calendar months commencing and counting backwards from the relevant date, i.e. the date of retrenchment. If he has, 
he would be deemed to be in continuous service for a period of one year for the purpose of section 25B and 
Chapter VA.” 


Thus, in view of the law laid down by the Hon’ble Apex Court as discussed above the initial burden of proof lies 
upon the Workman to show that he has completed 240 days of the service with the Respondent just preceding from 
the date of his termination. Further, in respect of the employment of calculating the 240 days service provision 
contained under Section 25-F read with Section 25-B of the I.D. Act, 947.

Further, Respondent contended that on 27.2.!997 a memorandum of understanding was also signed between the 
Federation’s affiliate and the bank management regarding the fact that the exercise of identifying the messengerial 
vacancies as on 3!.!2.994 has since been completed by central office and thereby 403 messengerial vacancies were 
sanctioned to the circle of the Management bank and it was agreed that these vacancies may be filled from 989 panel 
of temporary employees after effecting conversion from full time non-messengerial staff in the usual manner and the 
agreement was reached upon. Further, it was agreed between the Federations affiliate and the management bank 
that in terms of the settlement dated 30.7.996 both the panels of temporary employees and daily wagers /casual 
employees would lapse on 3.3.997. 


उप. The Workman has contended that the empanelled list prepared by the Respondent management for 
appointment of temporary and daily wage Workers to the permanent post cannot lapse unless until it is exhausted by 
appointing all the empanelled persons and it should continue even after 3.3.997, i.e., the date fixed for the lapse of 
panel. It is undisputed that the date of lapse of empanelled list of Workmen has been fixed to 3.3.997 as 
mentioned in the settlement dated 30.7.996, and agreed between the parties. It is settled law that and once the life 
of panel list lapses on the date as agreed between the parties it cannot be extended beyond that date. In the instant 
case the panel list of the workmen was valid upto 3.3.997 in view of the terms and conditions enumerated in the 5" 
Settlement entered into between the parties. As the lapse of panel i.e., 3.3.997 has been agreed by State Bank of 
India and State Bank of India Staff Federation through 5‘ Settlement, the Workman is not competent to challenge the 
same. 


In this context I would like to take reference of the decision of the apex court in the case of Syndicate Bank and Ors 
vs. Shankar Paul and Ors , AIR 997 SC 309], therein the Hon’ble Apex Court have held:- 


“Till 7962, the branches of the appellant Bank in Calcutta region were recruiting persons locally to work as 
temporary attenders in leave vacancies. In view of the revised procedure prescribed by the Government of India in 
respect of such temporary appointments, the Calcutta regional office of the appellant Bank issued a circular to all of 
its branches on /4.6./9862, instructing all the branches under it to discontinue the old practice from /.6./982 and 
appoint only empanelled candidates. The regional office was to prepare a panel of eligible candidates, after calling 
names from the local/district employment exchange, and split it up branch-wise. Following that new procedure yearly 
panels were prepared thereafter. Names of the Respondents were for the first time included in the panel prepared for 
the period 7.2. /967 to 6.2. /966, By its letter dated 7.2, /967 the Bank had informed the Respondents that the panel 
was valid for one year only and that inclusion of their names in the panel was not to confer on them any right to seek 
permanent appointment in the service of the bank. Considering the object with which the panel was prepared and the 
fact that it was an yearly panel expiring on 6.2, /966, we are of the opinion that the Respondents did not get any right, 
because of inclusion of their names in the said panel, for permanent absorption in the service of the Bank. Whatever 
conditional right they had came to an end with the expiry of the panel. The claim of the Respondents, as contained in 
the writ petition was thus misconceived and therefore the learned single Judge and the Division Bench, when it first 
decided the appeal, were right in dismissing the writ petition and the appeal respectively.” 


Thus, in view of the above law laid down by the Hon’ble Apex Court and in view of the terms and conditions of the 
5" Settlement the contention of the Workman that empanelled list should continue even after 3.3.997 till the last 
Workman in the panel is absorbed is not tenable. The contention of the Workman is baseless in view of recital in 
the settlement. Therefore, in view of the fore gone discussion and finding given at Point No. I regarding binding 
nature of Settlements and terms and conditions enumerated therein, in view of the provision contained u/s.|8() of the 
ILD. Act, 947, I am of the considered view that life of panels lapsed on 3.3.997 in view of terms of settlement 
dated 30.7.996 and plea of Workman that the panel shall continue even after 3.3.]997 till last man absorbed has 
no legal force and same is untenable. 


[भाग ए---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मार्च 28, 2026/चैत्र 7, 948 2029 


38. Undisputedly, settlement agreement dated 30.7.996 was executed between the State Bank of India and 
State Bank of India Staff Federation and in that settlement it was agreed that both the panels of temporary employees 
and daily wagers/ casual employees will be used for filling vacancies existing as on 3.2.994 as per the norms 
agreed between the bank and the Federation. These empanelled workmen were to be given a chance for permanent 
appointment in the bank against vacancies arising up to December 994 whereas the daily wagers/ casual employees 
were to be considered against the vacancies arise from January 995 to December !996, whereby the said panel 
would lapse. It was agreed that the vacancies falls upto 3.3.!997 shall be filled before the empanelled list is 
allowed to lapse. Thus, the claim of the Workman to the post of permanent non-messenger in the Respondent 
management was subject to the availability of the sanctioned post and vacancies arising upto 3.3.997. The 
workmen given chance to the permanent post were seniors in number of working days in panel list and Workman 
herein was junior to those workmen. Therefore, Workman could not be given absorption to permanent post being 
junior to other workmen in the panel list. 


39. In this context the Workman witness १७] was cross examined by the Respondent counsel and in the cross 
examination the witness WW] states:- 


“I applied in response to an advertisement given by the bank in terms of the settlements entered into by the union 
with the bank. .... Further, witness states, I do not know that the names were included in the panel basing upon the 
no. of days of service put in by the temporary employees. I do not know that the temporary employees whose names 
were included in the panel were given regular appointment basing on their seniority depending upon the no. of days 
of service put in by them as per the notification....” 


Thus, from the above statement of the Workman witness १४७] it is clear that the panel was prepared in terms of 
various settlements entered into between Staff Federation of State Bank of India and State Bank of India and it was 
prepared on the basis of number of days of work put in by the temporary employees. Further, the Workman himself 
admitted that some of the temporary employees whose names were included in the panel were given regular 
appointment in the bank in order of their seniority in the panel and he is not having any document to show that any 
person who worked for less number of days than the Workman was given appointment in the bank. Therefore, the 
allegation of the Workman that the regular appointment has been made by the bank from the panel list in breach of 
the terms of the settlement and violation of seniority of panel list is not proved by this evidence of WWI. Thus, 
there is no evidence on record that bank has given the appointment to the temporary employees as well as daily 
wagers from the panel list 989 and 992 in breach of seniority of the temporary employees in the list. There is no 
evidence of jumbling in the panel list to make appointment of any permanent Workman in breach of the seniority. 
Therefore, I am constrained to hold that the Respondent Management has appointed the workmen from panel list in 
order of seniority and there is no jumbling of workmen in the panel list before it got lapsed on 3.3.997, 


40. However, Workman has taken the plea that the panels of Workmen for absorption in the employment of the 
Respondent banks (panels of temporary employees and daily wagers) has been lapsed on 3.3.997 in contravention 
of terms of settlement as the object of preparing the entire empanelment of temporary and daily wagers was to 
provide them permanent employment and till the both the panel lists exhausted the panel list cannot be lapsed on 
3.3.997 and the date of lapsing of the panel on 3.3.997 has been fixed by the Respondent arbitrarily without any 
authority. 


4l. In this context, the perusal of Settlement dated 30.7.996 reveals that the 5" Settlement dated 30.7.996 
was entered under Section 2(p) and 8(l) of I.D. Act, 947 read with Rule 58 of Industrial Dispute (Central) Rules 
957. This settlement has been entered into by the competent parties and in this settlement parties thereto agreed 
that both the panels of temporary employees and daily wagers/casual employees will lapse on 3.3.997. Thus the 
date of lapse of panel was fixed by both the parties with consensus under the settlement dated 30.7.996 and same is 
binding upon the Workman under the provision of Section 8() of LD. Act, 947. Moreover, this issue of binding 
force of the settlement dated 7..987, 6.7.988, 27.0.988 and 9..99 has already been discussed, decided at 
finding in Point No.I of this award. However, the legality and validity of the aforementioned settlement has not been 
challenged by the Workman before any competent forum. Thus, claim of Workman that the date of lapse of panel 
i.e., 3.3.997 has been fixed arbitrarily by the Respondent bank is untenable. As regard the claim of Workman for 
his absorption to the permanent post it is settled law that the Workman can not claim his regularization to permanent 
post merely on the basis of number of working days. 


42. In this context the reference of the decision of Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Oil and Natural Gas 
Corporation vs Krishan Gopal 2020(3) SCALE 272, date of decision 7.2.2020 is relevant therein Hon’ble 
Supreme Court have has laid down principle regarding regularization of the Workman on permanent posts. Hon’ble 
Supreme Court have laid down the prepositions of regularization of the workmen to permanent post is as under:- 


“(i) Wide as they are, the powers of the Labour Court and the Industrial Court cannot extend to a direction to order 
regularisation, where such a direction would in the context of public employment offend the provisions contained 
in Article /4 of the Constitution; 


2030 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MARCH 28, 2026/CHAITRA 7, 948 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


(ii) The statutory power of the Labour Court or Industrial Court to grant relief to workmen including the status of 
permanency continues to exist in circumstances where the employer has indulged in an unfair labour practice by not 
filling up permanent posts even though such posts are available and by continuing to employ workmen as temporary 
or daily wage employees despite their performing the same work as regular workmen on lower wages; 


(iii) The power to create permanent or sanctioned posts lies outside the judicial domain and where no posts are 
available, a direction to grant regularisation would be impermissible merely on the basis of the number of years of 
service; 


(iv) Where an employer has regularised similarly situated workmen either in a scheme or otherwise, it would be open 
to workmen who have been deprived of the same benefit at par with the workmen who have been regularised to make 
a complaint before the Labour or Industrial Court, since the deprivation of the benefit would amount to a violation of 
Article /4, and 


(v) In order to constitute an unfair labour practice under Section 2(ra) read with Item /09 of the Vth Schedule of the 
ID Act, the employer should be engaging workmen as badlis, temporaries or casuals, and continuing them for years, 
with the object of depriving them of the benefits payable to permanent workmen. 


Thus, in view of the principles laid down by the Hon’ble Supreme Court as discussed above, in the instant matter the 
Workman utterly failed to prove his claim by adducing any documentary or oral evidence that the employer has 
indulged in unfair labour practice by not filling the permanent posts even though such posts are available and by 
continuing to employ workmen as temporary or daily wage employees despite their performance was the same work, 
as regular workmen on lower wages. 


43. Respondent has contended that all the vacancies exist and arise upto 3!.3.997 has been filled up from the 
panel list in order of seniority and no vacancy exists or arises as on 3.3.997 remained unfilled. Further, it is 
contended that as per terms of settlement the life of panel lists has been lapsed on 3.3.997, hence, there is no 
occasion to extend the life of panel lists beyond 3.3.!997. However, the workman failed to prove contrary by any 
evidence to the aforesaid contention of the Respondent that the vacancies were existing as on 3!.3.997 and the 
workman was not given absorption to the permanent post in order of his seniority. It is settled law that the power to 
create permanent or sanctioned post lies outside the judicial domain and where no posts are available, a direction to 
grant regularization would be impermissible merely on the basis of the number of years of service. Therefore, the 
claim of the workman on this ground also not acceptable. 


44. Further, as per the of settlement, panel was prepared for absorption of the workmen on the permanent posts 
has already been lapsed on 3!.3.997 and the vacancies existing and arising upto 3.2.994 and upto 3.3.997 as 
settlement dated 30.7.996 has been filled up from the panel by appointing the workmen as per seniority in the panel 
list. Workman witness WW in his cross examination has himself admitted this fact that, some of the temporary 
employees whose names were included in the panel were given regular appointment in the bank in order of their 
seniority in the panel. The Workman failed to show that there was any breach of terms of settlement has been 
committed by the Respondent in appointment to permanent post from aforesaid panel list. 


45. As discussed in preceding paragraph of this Award, the life of the panel has not been extended beyond 
3.3.997, by any further settlement hence, the panel list in which name of the Workman was included got expired 
on 3I.3.997. It is not the case of the Workman that Respondent has regularized similarly situated workmen either in 
the scheme or otherwise and the Workman has been deprived of same benefit on par with those workmen or the 
vacancies remained unfilled on the date of lapse of panels i.e., 3.3.997, Industrial Tribunal has no jurisdiction to 
extend the date of lapse of panel i.e., 3.3.997. This Tribunal can not order for regularization of workmen to the 
permanent post in contravention of the provision of Article l4 of the Constitution of India. 


In the case of Mahboob Deepak vs. Nagar Panchayat Gajraula & Anr, Civil Appeal No.5875/2007 date of 
judgement 3.2.2007, Hon’ble Supreme Court have held:- 


“8. Respondent is a Local Authority. The terms and conditions of employment of the employees are governed by a 
statute and statutory rules. No appointment can be made by a Local Authority without following the provisions of the 
recruitment rules. Any appointment made in violation of the said rules as also the constitutional scheme of equality as 
contained in Articles /4 and /6 of the Constitution of India would be a nullity. 


9. Due to some exigency of work, although recruitment on daily wages or on an ad hoc basis was permissible, but by 
reason thereof an employee cannot claim any right to be permanently absorbed in service or made permanent in 
absence of any statute or statutory rules. Merely because an employee has completed 240 days of work in a year 
preceding the date of retrenchment, the same would not mean that his services were liable to be regularized.” 


Therefore, in view of the law laid down by the Hon’ble Apex Court, the claim of the Workman for absorption merely 
on the basis of number of day of work in the Respondent bank Branch is not acceptable. As regard plea of the 
Workman that the Workman should have been given employment even after 3.3.997 as temporary Workman, it is 
the discretion of Respondent to engage the Workman depending upon availability of work and this Tribunal can not 
direct the Respondent to engage the Workman in the absent of such rule/scheme. 


[भाग ए---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मार्च 28, 2026/चैत्र 7, 948 203 


46. In view of principle laid down by Hon’ble Apex Court as discussed above, in the instant matter Workman 
utterly failed to establish the fact of rendering continuous service for a period of 240 days of service within a period 
of 2 calendar months commencing and coming backward from relevant date i.e., the date of retrenchment, if has he 
would be denied to be in continuous service for a period of one year. Therefore, the provision contained under 
Sec.25F of retrenchment is not applicable to Workman. 


Counsel for Workman has relied upon number of decisions of Hon’ble High Court and Hon'ble Supreme Court and 
few of them are discussed herein:- 


In the case of F.C.I., vs. Kamdhenu Cattle Feed Industries 993 () SCC 7], therein Hon’ble Supreme Court have 
held:- 


“7. In contractual sphere as in all other State actions, the State and all its instrumentalities have to conform to Article 
_4 of the Constitution of which non-arbitrariness is a significant facet. There is no unfettered discretion in public law: 
A public authority possesses powers only to use them for public good. This impose the duty to act fairly and to adopt 
a procedure which is ‘fairplay in action’. Due observance of this obligation as a part of good administration raises a 
reasonable or legitimate expectation in every citizen to be treated fairly in his interaction with the State and its 
instrumentalities, with this element forming a necessary component of the decision making process in all State 
actions. To satisfy this requirement of non- arbitrariness in a State action, it is, therefore, necessary to consider and 
give due weight to the reasonable or legitimate expectations of the persons likely lo be affected by the decision or else 
that unfairness in the exercise of the power may amount to an abuse or excess of power apart from affecting the bona 
fides of the decision in a given case. The decision so made would be exposed to challenge on the ground of 
arbitrariness. Rule of law does not completely eliminate discretion in the exercise of power, as it is unrealistic, but 
providers for control of its exercise by judicial review.” 


In the case of State Bank of India, R.O., Vijayawada vs. Industrial Tribunal, Hyderabad WP १४०.।9३/997, 
therein Hon’ble High Court have held, 


“Sri Krovvidi Narasimham, the learned counsel for the 2" respondent contends, supporting the award that it was a 
permanent vacancy and even though the 2" respondent was appointed on temporary basis, his services were not 
liable to be terminated and he was to be regularised into service on permanent basis. Shastry award warrants that no 
temporary appointment can be made to a permanent post. But the matter is now covered by two division bench 
judgements dated 26, //./986 in W.A. No.79 of /966 and 25.6. /967 in W.A. No.270 of /962, The ratio decided in the 
two judgements is to the effect that there cannot be any mandate to appoint employees on permanent basis when the 
requirement was for appointment on temporary basis. But it is held in the said judgements that when a temporary 
appointee is ousted from service and not for misconduct and, if again temporary appointment is to be made, then, the 
case of such temporary appointee who was ousted, has got to be considered in accordance with Sec. 25-H of 
the Act.” 


In the case of State of Haryana and others vs. Piara Singh and others. 992 (4) SCC 8, therein Hon’ble 
Supreme Court have held:- 


“ 49. If for any reason an adhoc or temporary employee is continued for a fairly long spell, the authorities must 
consider his case for regularization provided he is eligible and qualified according to the rules and his service record 
is satisfactory and his appointment does not run counter to the reservation policy of the state.” 


In the above cited judgements by the Workman the facts of the case are different hence do not apply to instant case 
of Workman. 


47. On the other hand, in support of his contention Respondent has examined witness MWI and ४५७४] in chief

Ex.M6 is the copy of the settlement dated 30.7.996. Further, witness states that on 27.2.!997 a memorandum of

The Government of India, Ministry of Labour by its order No. L-!20l2/359/2000-IR(B.IT) — dated

2. Before unfolding the factual matrix of the instant industrial dispute it would be apposite to have a bird eye

4. Now the Authority constituted under Section 4/(/) of the Act is an authority with very limited jurisdiction. It can 
only decide in the first appeal whether a termination by the management is valid or not and is within the parameters 
of Section 40 of the Act. The said Authority, in our view, has absolutely no jurisdiction to decide whether a settlement 
entered into under Section /0(/) of the Industrial Disputes Act between the representatives of the Workmen and of the

Authority, namely, the Assistant Commissioner of Labour, was never intended by the A.P. Legislature to have 
jurisdiction to go into the question of the validity of a settlement arrived at under Section /6 of the Industrial Disputes

Act, with extensive powers cannot be disputed. What we mean to say is that the Authority under Section 476) of the 
A.P. Act has no jurisdiction what-so-ever either to question or to decide about the validity of any such settlements. If 
parties to a settlement have a grievance about the validity of a settlement, it is for them to agitate the matter before

The Tribunal thought that the question of the quantum of membership of the 2nd Respondent did not call for a finding

“When a recognised union negotiates with an employer the workers as individuals do not come into the picture. It is 
not necessary that each individual worker should know the implications of the settlement since a recognised union,

which is expected to protect the legitimate interests of labour, enters into a settlement in the best interests of labour.

President of the 3rd Respondent in this case. That being the position, prima facie, this is a settlement in the course of

It is not possible to scan the settlement in bits and pieces and hold some parts good and acceptable and others bad. 
Unless it can be demonstrated that the objectionable portion is such that it completely outweighs all the other

Compensation to workmen in case of transfer of undertakings. 
Section 25B defines the term continuous service which provides 


Definition of continuous service.- For the purposes of this Chapter,--

(2) a Workman shall be said to be in continuous service for a period if he is, for that period, in uninterrupted service,

(a) for a period of one year, if the Workman, during a period of twelve calendar months preceding the date with

In order to prove the fact of 240 days of service within !2 months of a calendar year just preceding from the date of

Further, how to calculate 240 days of service by the Workman in a calendar year. In this context the reference of 
decisions of Hon’ble Supreme Court is relevant and the same are discussed below:- 


In Rajasthan State Ganganagar S. Mills Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan and Anr. (2004) Apex Court held: 


"It was the case of the Workman that he had worked for more than 240 days in the year concerned. This claim was 
denied by the appellant. It was for the claimant to lead evidence to show that he had worked for 240 days in the year 
preceding the date of his termination. He has filed an affidavit. It is statement which is in his favor and that cannot be 
regarded as sufficient evidence for any Court or Tribunal to come to the conclusion that in fact the claimant had 
worked for 240 days in a year These aspects were highlighted in Range Forest Officer v. S.T. Hadimani (2002 (3) 
SCC 25. No proof of receipt of salary or wages for 240 days or order or record in that regard was produced. Mere 
non-production of the muster roll for a particular period was not sufficient for the Labour Court held that the 
Workman had worked for 240 days as claimed." 


In Municipal Corporation, Faridabad v. Siri Niwas (2004 (8) SCC 95), held "the burden was on the Workman to 
show that he was working for more than 240 days in the preceding one year prior to his alleged retrenchment." In 
MP. Electricity Board v. Hariram (2004 (8) SCC 246) the position was again reiterated in paragraph I] as follows: 
"The above burden having not been discharged and the Labour Court having held so, in our opinion, the Industrial 
Court and the High Court erred in basing an order of reinstatement solely on an adverse inference drawn 
erroneously ..” 


In the case of Manager, RBI, Bangalore vs. S Mani (2005) SCC Page 00, the 3 Judges Bench of the Apex 
Court held that "the initial burden of proof was on the Workman to show that he had completed 240 days of service." 


Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Mohan Lal vs Management BEL 98 SCC page 225 has laid down the 
principle that how to count 240 days of service within one year itis held: "Clause (2)(a) provides for a fiction 
to treat a Workman in continuous service for a period of one year despite the fact that he has not rendered 
uninterrupted service for a period of one year but he has rendered period of 240 days during the period of /2 
calendar service for months counting backwards and just preceding the relevant date being the date of retrenchment. 
In other words, in order to invoke the fiction enacted in clause (2)(a) it is necessary to determine first the relevant 
date, ie the date of termination of service which is complained of as retrenchment. After that date is ascertained. move 
backward to a period of /2 months just preceding the date of retrenchment and then ascertain whether within the 
period of /2 months, the Workman has rendered service for a period of 240 days. If these three facts are affirmatively 
answered in favor of the Workman pursuant to the deeming fiction enacted in clause (2)(a) it will have to be assumed 
that the Workman is in continuous service for a period of one year and he will satisfy the eligibility qualification 
enacted in Section 25-F" 


“4, We have already extracted section 25B since its amendment and the change in language is the legislative 
exposition of which note must be taken. In fact, we need not further dilate upon this aspect because in Surendra 
Kumar Verma_and Ors. v. Central Government Industrial-cum-Labour Court, New Delhi and Anr., Chinnappa 
Reddy. J., after noticing the amendment and referring to the decision in Sur_Enamel and Stamping Works (P) 
Ltd case, held as under: 


"These changes brought about by Act 36 of /964 appear to be clearly designed to provide that a Workman who has 
actually worked under the employer for not less than 240 days during a period of twelve months shall be deemed to 
have been in continuous service for a period of one year whether or not he has in fact been in such continuous service 
for a period of one year. It is enough that he has worked for 240 days in a period of 2 months, it is not necessary that 
he should have been in the service of the employer for one whole year." 


In a concurring judgment Pathak J. agreed with this interpretation of section 25B(2). Therefore, both on principle 
and on precedent it must be held that section 25B(2) comprehends a situation where a Workman is not in employment

for a period of 72 calendar months, but has rendered service for a period of 240 days within the period of

has, he would be deemed to be in continuous service for a period of one year for the purpose of section 25B and

Thus, in view of the law laid down by the Hon’ble Apex Court as discussed above the initial burden of proof lies

37. The Workman has contended that the empanelled list prepared by the Respondent management for 
appointment of temporary and daily wage Workers to the permanent post cannot lapse unless until it is exhausted by

In this context I would like to take reference of the decision of the apex court in the case of Syndicate Bank and Ors 
vs. Shankar Paul and Ors , AIR 997 SC 309, therein the Hon’ble Apex Court have held:- 


“Till 7962, the branches of the appellant Bank in Calcutta region were recruiting persons locally to work as 
temporary attenders in leave vacancies. In view of the revised procedure prescribed by the Government of India in 
respect of such temporary appointments, the Calcutta regional office of the appellant Bank issued a circular to all of 
its branches on /4.6./982, instructing all the branches under it to discontinue the old practice from /.6./982 and 
appoint only empanelled candidates. The regional office was to prepare a panel of eligible candidates, after calling 
names from the local/district employment exchange, and split it up branch-wise. Following that new procedure yearly 
panels were prepared thereafter. Names of the Respondents were for the first time included in the panel prepared for 
the period 7.2. /967 to 6.2. /966, By its letter dated 7.2./967 the Bank had informed the Respondents that the panel 
was valid for one year only and that inclusion of their names in the panel was not to confer on them any right to seek 
permanent appointment in the service of the bank. Considering the object with which the panel was prepared and the 
fact that it was an yearly panel expiring on 6.2, /966, we are of the opinion that the Respondents did not get any right, 
because of inclusion of their names in the said panel, for permanent absorption in the service of the Bank. Whatever 
conditional right they had came to an end with the expiry of the panel. The claim of the Respondents, as contained in 
the writ petition was thus misconceived and therefore the learned single Judge and the Division Bench, when it first 
decided the appeal, were right in dismissing the writ petition and the appeal respectively.” 


Thus, in view of the above law laid down by the Hon’ble Apex Court and in view of the terms and conditions of the 
5" Settlement the contention of the Workman that empanelled list should continue even after 3.3.997 till the last

dated 30.7.996 and plea of Workman that the panel shall continue even after 3.3.997 till last man absorbed has 
no legal force and same is untenable.

42. In this context the reference of the decision of Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Oil and Natural Gas 
Corporation vs Krishan Gopal 2020(3) SCALE 272, date of decision 7.2.2020 is relevant therein Hon’ble 
Supreme Court have has laid down principle regarding regularization of the Workman on permanent posts. Hon’ble 
Supreme Court have laid down the prepositions of regularization of the workmen to permanent post is as under:- 


“(i) Wide as they are, the powers of the Labour Court and the Industrial Court cannot extend to a direction to order 
regularisation, where such a direction would in the context of public employment offend the provisions contained 
in Article /4 of the Constitution; 


(ti) The statutory power of the Labour Court or Industrial Court to grant relief to workmen including the status of 
permanency continues to exist in circumstances where the employer has indulged in an unfair labour practice by not 
filling up permanent posts even though such posts are available and by continuing to employ workmen as temporary 
or daily wage employees despite their performing the same work as regular workmen on lower wages; 


(tii) The power to create permanent or sanctioned posts lies outside the judicial domain and where no posts are 
available, a direction to grant regularisation would be impermissible merely on the basis of the number of years of 
service; 


(iv) Where an employer has regularised similarly situated workmen either in a scheme or otherwise, it would be open 
to workmen who have been deprived of the same benefit at par with the workmen who have been regularised to make 
a complaint before the Labour or Industrial Court, since the deprivation of the benefit would amount to a violation of 
Article /4, and 


(v) In order to constitute an unfair labour practice under Section 2(ra) read with Item /09 of the Vth Schedule of the 
ID Act, the employer should be engaging workmen as badlis, temporaries or casuals, and continuing them for years, 
with the object of depriving them of the benefits payable to permanent workmen. 


Thus, in view of the principles laid down by the Hon’ble Supreme Court as discussed above, in the instant matter the 
Workman utterly failed to prove his claim by adducing any documentary or oral evidence that the employer has 
indulged in unfair labour practice by not filling the permanent posts even though such posts are available and by 
continuing to employ workmen as temporary or daily wage employees despite their performance was the same work, 
as regular workmen on lower wages.

grant regularization would be impermissible merely on the basis of the number of years of service. Therefore, the

In the case of Mahboob Deepak vs. Nagar Panchayat Gajraula & Anr, Civil Appeal No.5875/2007 date of 
judgement 3.2.2007, Hon’ble Supreme Court have held:- 


“8. Respondent is a Local Authority. The terms and conditions of employment of the employees are governed by a 
statute and statutory rules. No appointment can be made by a Local Authority without following the provisions of the 
recruitment rules. Any appointment made in violation of the said rules as also the constitutional scheme of equality as 
contained in Articles /4 and /6 of the Constitution of India would be a nullity. 


9. Due to some exigency of work, although recruitment on daily wages or on an ad hoc basis was permissible, but by 
reason thereof an employee cannot claim any right to be permanently absorbed in service or made permanent in 
absence of any statute or statutory rules. Merely because an employee has completed 240 days of work in a year 
preceding the date of retrenchment, the same would not mean that his services were liable to be regularized.”

the discretion of Respondent to engage the Workman depending upon availability of work and this Tribunal can not

Counsel for Workman has relied upon number of decisions of Hon’ble High Court and Hon'ble Supreme Court and

In the case of F.C.I., vs. Kamdhenu Cattle Feed Industries 993 () SCC 7], therein Hon’ble Supreme Court have 
held:- 


“7. In contractual sphere as in all other State actions, the State and all its instrumentalities have to conform to Article 
34० the Constitution of which non-arbitrariness is a significant facet. There is no unfettered discretion in public law: 
A public authority possesses powers only to use them for public good. This impose the duty to act fairly and to adopt 
a procedure which is ‘fairplay in action’. Due observance of this obligation as a part of good administration raises a 
reasonable or legitimate expectation in every citizen to be treated fairly in his interaction with the State and its 
instrumentalities, with this element forming a necessary component of the decision making process in all State 
actions. To satisfy this requirement of non- arbitrariness in a State action, it is, therefore, necessary to consider and 
give due weight to the reasonable or legitimate expectations of the persons likely lo be affected by the decision or else 
that unfairness in the exercise of the power may amount to an abuse or excess of power apart from affecting the bona 
fides of the decision in a given case. The decision so made would be exposed to challenge on the ground of 
arbitrariness. Rule of law does not completely eliminate discretion in the exercise of power, as it is unrealistic, but 
providers for control of its exercise by judicial review.” 


In the case of State Bank of India, R.O., Vijayawada vs. Industrial Tribunal, Hyderabad WP १४०.93/997,

“Sri Krovvidi Narasimham, the learned counsel for the 2"4 respondent contends, supporting the award that it was a

appointee is ousted from service and not for misconduct and, if again temporary appointment is to be made, then, the 
case of such temporary appointee who was ousted, has got to be considered in accordance with Sec. 25-H of 
the Act.”

“Whether the claim of Sh. Ramesh S/o Late Shri Ram Krishna for compassionate appointment with the 
management of Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd., New Delhi is maintainable? If yes, what relief the claimant 
is entitled to? 


The claimant seeks appointment with the management on compassionate grounds in lieu of the services 
rendered by Late Sh. Ram Kishan, who passed away on 2..2000 during the course of his employment. He submits 
that after his father’s death, the family became helpless, as his father was the single bread earner. He tried to find a 
job but was unsuccessful. He further stated that after his father’s death, he applied for compassionate appointment 
07.0I.200l and again on 23.0.200l, but both requests were denied. Another application dated 23.0!.200l was 
submitted by his mother, which was also not considered. His mother expired on 3.02.2009, and he has no source of 
income to support his family. The claimant later sent a demand letter dated 30.07.20l5, which remained unanswered 
by the management, following which he filed the present claim. 


In response, the management filed a written statement taking a preliminary objection that the dispute is not 
an industrial dispute or individual dispute as defined under section 2(k) and 2A of the Act. It relied upon the 
judgment of Hon’ble Supreme Court of India in Union of India and Ors. vs. Sima Banerjee, in Civil Appeal no. 257 
of 2077 passed on 0.0!.20l7, wherein it was held that the object of compassionate appointment is to enable the 
family to tide over the sudden crisis, anda direction to provide appointment several years after death is not justified. 


It was submitted that the claimant approached the conciliation officer, nearly after l6-l7 years after the 
rejection of his request. The management further submitted that the claimant’s family owned substantial land and 
earned a handsome income from it, and therefore was not in poor circumstances. Further, it is submitted that a letter 
in regard to compassionate appointment was received and duly processed by the management. The application was 
considered in accordance with the existing policies/schemes/rules. A discreet enquiry was conducted by the 
management, during which it was found that the claimant’s family had sufficient income from agriculture activities. 
Based on the findings of the enquiry report, the application for appointment on compassionate grounds was rejected 
by the management vide its letter dated 9.0.200]. 


Subsequently, upon receiving a representation from National Commission for SC/ST, the matter was further 
deliberated. Vide letter dated 05..200l, the commission was formally informed of the rejection of the claimant’s 
request for appointment on compassionate grounds. 


It is also important to mention herein that when the claim was filed in the year 209, the management failed 
to appear initially and was proceeded ex-parte. However, the management appeared on 4.!0.2024 after service of 
notice. Subsequently, it filed an application for setting aside the ex-parte order, which was allowed. The written 
statement was filed thereafter. 


During the course of proceedings, certain facts emerged. The claimant is 54 years old at present. At the time 
of his father’s death, he was about 30 years old. Upon being asked, he was unable to clarify whether he was married 
at the time of his father’s death or whether he had children. The eldest child is thirty years old at present. He didn’t 
disclose the date of his marriage. The remaining three children are aged 22 years, 5 years and l0 years old 
respectively. However, the exact dates of birth of these children has not been disclosed. Based on the information 
furnished by the claimant that the eldest child is around thirty years old, it is presumed that the marriage solemnized 
before 995. 


The record further reveals that in 200l, he submitted that an application for appointment on compassionate 
grounds with the management. The application was subsequently rejected by the management after review of all 
relevant details. Further, in a letter dated 05..200l addressed to Sh. Sohanlal, Assistant Commissioner, National 
Commission for SC/ST, 5" Floor, Lok Nayak Bhawan, Khan Market, New Delhi-l0003, the management stated that 
after discreet enquiries, it was found that eldest son of the deceased employee was engaged in agricultural activities 
and earning a regular income . It was also noted that all dependents were married. The management clarified that it 
considers appointment only in cases, where no other family member remains to support the family after the death of 
the bread earner. 


In this respect, the compassionate appointment policy for Public Sector General Insurance Companies 
including the Oriental Insurance Company Ltd.) based on the Model Scheme for Compassionate Appointment as 
circulated by the Ministry of Finance (Department of Financial Services) vide F.No. 404/02/20i2-Ins.II 
dated 7th August 20I4 is applicable. The key portions of the circular state: 


"The Government has considered the matter and has decided that all Public Sector General Insurance 
Companies may consider implementing a scheme for compassionate appointment of dependents of 
employees who die in harness or retire on medical grounds, in line with the scheme of Public Sector Banks 
as approved by the Government. 


[भाग ए---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मार्च 28, 2026/चैत्र 7, 948 2053 


... The scheme for compassionate appointment should provide for appointment of dependents of employees dying in 
harness and those retiring on medical grounds, subject to the following conditions and as per the Model Scheme: 


a) Limit on appointment: The number of appointments under the scheme to be restricted to 5% of the total 
vacancies in a year in each company for direct recruitment in Group 'C' posts... 


b) Eligibility: The scheme should provide for appointment of the spouse, son, daughter (including adopted 
son/daughter) or, in case the deceased employee was unmarried, the dependent brother or sister. 


c) Cut-off date and _non-retrospective effect: The scheme will be effective from the date of approval of the 
Board of the respective public sector general insurance company. Cases prior to such approval shall not be 
eligible for consideration unless otherwise specified..." 


d) Time frame: Applications for compassionate appointment must generally be made within five years of the 
date of death or retirement on medical grounds. 


e) Discretionary nature: Appointment on compassionate grounds is not a matter of right, but subject to 
availability of vacancy and fulfillment of conditions prescribed under the Scheme. " 


In cases where the applicant is married, greater scrutiny is required. In the present case, the claimant was married 6-7 
years prior to his father’s death and had children. Thus, it cannot be said that the applicant was dependent on his 
father’s income at that time. Further, the claim was filed after an excessive delay of sixteen years with no valid 
explanation for the delay. The initial rejection of his application was not even disclosed in the reference. 


In light of the above findings, the reference is answered against the claimant and in favor of the management. 
Accordingly, the claim of the claimants stands dismissed. A copy of this award be sent to the appropriate government 
for notification under section 7 of the I.D Act. The case file is consigned to record room.

oe The facts in brief as stated by the Claimant in his statement of claim filed on 7.03.202] are as under:- 


(3) The claimant while working as Operator-cum-Technician (OCT) with the II[—Party/Management since

the charge sheet could not reach to him and an ex-parte inquiry was conducted and as per order dated 7.0.209,

(iii) The claimant further stated that even in the ex-parte inquiry, no material was taken on record with reference to 
the allegations of charge no.(b) and (d), as well as punishment of dismissal from service is shockingly

(iv) The claimant further stated that he was not appeared before the Inquiry Officer and did not offer any

(vi) The claimant took up conciliation petition dated 2.03.2020 before the Regional Labour Commissioner

3. On the other hand, a counter affidavit was filed by the II Party/Management and stated that claimant Shri

notice dated 04.04.209 (Annexure-l8) was issued and the claimant was called for enquiry on 0.04.209 at .00 
am in the office of the Enquiry Officer. But this letter was also returned with the remarks “addressee refused” 
(Annexure-l9). This letter was also pasted on notice board (Annexure-20). By following the principles of natural 
justice, one more last and final chance was given to Shri R.Senthil Kumar by issuing enquiry notice dated 
23.04.209 (Annexure-2) in which he was called upon to attend enquiry on 03.05.20l9 at I.00 am. This notice 
was received by the claimant (Annexure-22). However, he failed to attend the enquiry on 03.05.209. So, the 
Inquiry Officer decided to conduct the enquiry ex-parte and asked the Presenting Officer to present the case and after 
considering evidence, concluded the enquiry and on the basis of enquiry, Shri R.Senthil Kumar services were
